_comment: Economic calendar. Regenerated on a schedule and committed; the site only renders it. Times are UTC and only UTC — the renderer converts to the reader's own clock. See tools/econ-calendar.md.

banks.expect: Hiked 25bp on 16 Sep, with all 19 participants backing it. The minutes say most see another hike likely by year-end without naming a month; futures price 28 Oct as a hold at about 83%, with December the likelier move and about three more quarter-point hikes priced by June. Wednesday's ten-year auction cleared at 5.300% with firm demand after the yield touched 5.365%; CPI on the 14th comes next

Second hike of 2026 on 10 Sep, to a 2.50% deposit rate. September's flash HICP printed 3.8%, but French bond stress (the ten-year near 4.92%), Spain's snap election and weaker retail sales and German orders have cut the ECB path to about two and a half more hikes from three and a half. One house expects a pause on 29 October and a final 25bp hike in December; the accounts of 10 September are out today

Held 6–3 on 17 Sep. Gilt yields hit a 28-year high on 1 October and Catherine Mann said a hike is needed because financial conditions are not tight enough; markets discount about 30bp by the end of the year and roughly 90bp through 2027, with labour data on 20 October and CPI on the 21st before the November meeting

Hiked to 1.25% on 18 Sep, a 31-year high. Sources say the Bank may judge underlying inflation to have reached 2% in its outlook report on 29–30 October, while a sideways Tankan takes pressure off a back-to-back hike; board member Sato said on Wednesday she favours gradual hikes. USD/JPY is near 158.4 and August real cash earnings rose 1.5%, an eighth straight gain
Held for a seventh meeting. Minutes flag oil pass-through; about 59% priced for an October hike. The 28 October decision comes with a policy report and a press conference

Hiked 25bp to 4.60% on 29 Sep, unanimous, and said more may be needed — but Bullock disclosed the board discussed holding, and August CPI printed 4.0% with a soft 0.2% monthly trimmed mean. ANZ still calls November; the currency fell through $0.70

Held at 0% on 24 Sep and nudged the inflation forecast up to 0.7–0.8% on energy. September CPI printed 1.0%, exactly as expected; December's hike odds sit near 31% from 71% a week earlier. A weaker franc is doing what a hike would

events.note: A surplus of A$495 million, the smallest in years, with July revised down to A$1.35 billion. Exports to a China that shuts for Golden Week today; the Australian dollar sits at 70 cents.

1.0% after 0.8%, exactly as expected. The SNB held at 0% on 24 September with a 0.7–0.8% forecast; December's hike odds had already fallen to about 31% from 71% this week and an in-line print leaves them there.
The only large euro-area manufacturing sector comfortably above 50. It is also the one most exposed to the energy bill.
Reported before the open with a revenue forecast the market read as positive; technology led the S&P 500 on the day and the shares helped.

197,000 against 200,000 expected, with the prior week revised to 198,000 and the four-week average down to 200,000. Challenger layoff announcements fell 18% to 43,281. The labour market into payrolls is solid, not improving.

events.event: Fed's Barkin, Collins and Schmid speak
events.note: Three regional presidents on a panel before the ISM print. Schmid is a 2026 voter; all three have been on the hawkish side since the hike.

At the ESRB conference, the day after German inflation printed 3.3% and the day before the euro-area flash. October's ECB odds have halved to about 30% this week on the euro's slide; anything on 'measured steps' moves them.
The final read of the flash 57.0 that moved the ten-year 14.6bp on 23 September. Revisions to flash PMIs are usually small; this one will be read closely anyway.
A governor who voted for the hike. Speaks at the minute the ISM prints.

54.5 against 55.0 expected and 54.6 before — a ninth month of expansion, the longest run since 2022. New orders 55.3 from 53.7, backlogs 56.4 from 51.8, employment 52.7 from 51.2, production slower at 56.7, inventories back in contraction at 48.6, export orders 50.9. Demand held; the cost line is the story, below.

77.9 against 72.3 expected and 71.1 before, the highest since May and back to where it stood in March when the Iran war began; 58.6% of respondents paid more and none reported lower prices, with every one of the six largest industries citing increases. ISM named steel and aluminium, tariffs and petroleum products. The ten-year touched 5.344% within the hour.

Said any further adjustment should follow a careful look at data trends, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks, which the market read as the second member of the Fed's leadership in three days counselling patience. October's hike odds fell from about 33% to about 25% as he spoke; the two-year closed 9.6bp lower.

New York, the day before payrolls, alongside Cook. Williams has said he expects one more hike this year, sees inflation at 3.5% in 2026 and now expects larger and longer-lasting energy effects than he did in the spring.

Earnings of 48 cents beat the 44 cents expected but revenue fell 4% to $11.21 billion against $11.32 billion, with Greater China down 26% and Converse down 28%; gross margin rose 60bp to 42.8%. Guided fiscal 2027 revenue down high single digits and adjusted earnings to $1.15–1.35 against $1.67 expected, and announced a restructuring called Pace with about $2.5 billion of savings through 2031 and job cuts from 2027. The shares fell between 6% and 9% after hours, already down 44% this year.

Dallas, after the close. Said policy has been 'offsides' and that rates need to rise half a point or more, without a timeline, and noted higher yields may partly reflect term premium. A 2026 voter, and the most hawkish voice of the week.

2.7% headline and 2.7% core ex-fresh-food, against 2.3–2.4% expected and 1.8% before, the highest since November 2025; the core-core measure rose to 3.0% from 2.0%, its first 3-handle since August 2025, and the seasonally adjusted month was +0.6%. Part of it is Tokyo's free water and childcare subsidies falling out of the base, part is energy pass-through, and services inflation firmed. The yen strengthened to 157.8 and JGB yields fell; October is back in the BoJ conversation after Thursday's cautious summary of opinions.

3.8% against 3.6–3.7% expected and 3.2% in August, a three-year high; the monthly rate was +0.6%. Energy inflation rose to 18.8% from 14.3% and food and services edged up, but core held at 2.5%, as expected. The ECB meets on 29 October: Standard Chartered still expects the Governing Council to wait for December's projections, while others read the print as making an October move harder to rule out. The euro stayed near its lowest since May 2025.

events.event: Euro area core HICP, flash (Sep, y/y)

events.note: 3.0% against 3.2% expected and 3.1% before, the slowest annual pace since May 2021; the monthly gain was +0.1% against +0.3%. The wage channel the Fed worries about most is not the one that is hot, which is part of why October's hike odds fell on the day.

+29,000 against 90,000 in the Bloomberg survey (84,000 in others) and a revised 133,000 in August; August was cut from 162,000 and July turned to a 10,000 loss from a 21,000 gain, a net 60,000 downward revision. Private payrolls rose 46,000 against about 81,000 expected; health care added 23,000 and leisure 10,000. The three-month average is near 51,000. Goldman had flagged the late Labor Day as a drag on September. October's hike went to about 22% priced from 64% a week earlier; December remains the favoured date.
4.2% against 4.1% expected, with participation up to 61.8% from 61.6% and the labour force larger, so part of the rise is people entering, not people laid off. The broad U6 rate slipped to 7.6%.
+0.1% as expected, with July revised down to +0.8% from +0.9%. Strong electrical-equipment orders were offset by weaker commercial aircraft.

After the jobs data, repeated that the funds-rate range needs to rise by another 50 basis points, while saying higher market yields are already doing some of the tightening. Treasury yields, which had fallen on the report, closed higher.

events.event: US S&P Global composite PMI, final (Sep)
events.note: Composite 58.4 as expected; the services index was revised to 58.8 from a 58.7 flash, the fastest expansion in more than five years, and S&P Global's survey also pointed to inflation pressure.

54.9 against 55.0 expected and 55.4 before, a 27th month of expansion. Business activity fell to 56.5 from 61.7 and new orders to 59.8 from 60.9, but employment rose to 50.1 from 47.8, back above 50 for the first time in three months, and export orders fell into contraction at 46.9. The headline was soft; the prices line, below, was not.

74.0 against 73.3 expected and 72.6 before, the highest since July 2022. Fuel, shipping and interest costs were the most-cited pressures. The ten-year touched 5.349% within hours, its highest since 2002, and closed near 5.31%. Together with manufacturing prices paid at 77.9 last Thursday, both ISM surveys are pointing the same way.

Speaks after the Tokyo close. Sources say the Bank may judge that underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal in the outlook report for its 29–30 October meeting, though the Tankan showed corporate inflation moving sideways, which takes pressure off a back-to-back hike. The yen is near 158, the ten-year JGB yield about 3.1%, and the 10-year auction earlier today drew firmer demand than last month's.

0.8% against 1.0% expected, and July was revised down to 0.4% from 0.6%. Volumes rose 0.1% on the month against 0.2% expected, with automotive fuel down 1.9% as pump prices rose. German factory orders fell 10.6% in August, the most in seven months, the same morning; the euro still closed higher on French bond relief.

A $105.6 billion deficit against $102 billion expected, the widest since March 2025; July was revised to $92.8 billion from $88.6 billion. Imports rose 4.3% to a record $420.8 billion on crude oil, capital goods tied to the AI build-out and nonmonetary gold, while exports rose 1.4% to $315.2 billion. Capital Economics says third-quarter GDP growth will now come in well below its 4.0% forecast, closer to 2.5%.
The New York Fed president whose 'no need for urgency' on 29 September began the October repricing, a week on and after the payrolls miss. He has said he expects one more hike this year.
A non-voter in 2026 who said last week that policy is still slightly accommodative after the September hike. He speaks again on Thursday.

$58 billion at 4.932%, the highest since 4.995% in May 2006 and up from 4.474% last month. The bid-to-cover was 2.62 against a 2.64 average of the last ten and 2.72 last time, and indirect bidders took 57.6% against a 63% twelve-month average; it did clear at about the 4.934% when-issued yield. The ten-year closed near 5.27%, down about 4bp, on a day oil dipped and Treasuries found buyers.

Kansas City. Said inflation is 'frustrating' and must be fixed, that AI is now one of the largest drivers of it, and that the policy rate still has to rise even though higher long-term yields are weighing on parts of the economy. San Francisco's Daly said the same day that inflation may last longer than expected and that more hikes may be needed; Williams had said last week there was no urgency.

$39 billion at 5.300%, up from 4.834% last month and the highest since 2000 on CNBC's count. Demand was firmer than the three-year's: the bid-to-cover was 2.77 against 2.71 last time and a 2.52 ten-auction average, and indirect bidders took about 80% of the notes. The ten-year had touched 5.365% earlier in the day, its highest since 2002, and eased to about 5.28% after the result.

All 19 participants supported the September hike and most judged that another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end, though they stressed they approach each meeting with an open mind. Many said a higher path was prudent as insurance against persistent inflation, and inflation risks were seen as tilted up on energy prices and AI-related investment. The minutes gave no date; futures price the 28 October meeting as a hold at about 83%, with December the likelier hike. Treasury yields rose and the ten-year touched 5.365% before easing.
The calendar has Waller early Thursday; a Reuters note had placed him, Kashkari and Musalem on Wednesday, and no remarks from him were found overnight, so check the time before relying on it.

The record of the 10 September hike, three weeks before the 29 October decision. Since then euro-area inflation has printed 3.8%, French ten-year yields have neared 5% and the market has cut its ECB path to about two and a half more hikes from three and a half; how the Council weighed higher energy prices against slowing growth is the read.

$22 billion, the last of the week's three. The long bond touched 5.73% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002, and closed near 5.67%; the last auction cleared at 5.308%. The ten-year drew firm demand on Wednesday at 5.300%, so this is the test of the longest maturity.
St. Louis, the day after the FOMC minutes. Said on 29 September that policy is still slightly accommodative even after the hike.
The Bank of Canada is still at 2.25% with an October hike about 59% priced. A jobless rate at 6.4% is the argument against; oil pass-through is the argument for.
The first big airline of the season, reporting into jet fuel that has doubled in a year. Guidance on fuel and demand is the read, not the quarter.

The first October survey. September was 48.1 with one-year inflation expectations at 4.6% and five-year at 3.4%; the New York Fed's survey on Wednesday put one-year expectations at the highest in more than three years, so the expectations line is the one the Fed will read.

events.event: Columbus Day — US bond market closed
events.note: Equities trade; Treasuries and the banks do not. The IMF and World Bank annual meetings run in Washington through the week.
The record of the 29 September hike to 4.60%, which Bullock said followed a discussion of holding. The read is how close the vote was and whether the Board expects to move again before the year ends.
The record of the meeting that markets have at about 90% for a hike from 4.35%. How close the vote was, and what August's 4.6% unemployment did to it, is the read.
The final read of the flash due 30 September. Germany sits at 2.9% against a euro-area 3.2%, and the ECB has said no meeting is ruled out.

The start of the third-quarter reporting season, with Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Citigroup and BlackRock the same morning. FactSet has S&P 500 earnings growing about 29% for the quarter, a third straight quarter above 25%; the banks report into a curve at 5% and a financials sector that is flat on the year.

events.event: Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth Q3 earnings

events.note: The first full month of sales agreed at mortgage rates above 7%. August fell 2.0%.
Pushed back a week by the Golden Week holiday. Still under 1% while the US prints 3%-plus; the gap is the whole US–China rates and currency story.
3.4% in August with the monthly at +0.4%. The first CPI after the September hike, two weeks before the 28 October decision.
0.3% last month. The Fed is hiking against the risk that energy leaks into core; this is where it would show.
The anecdotal survey two weeks before the 28 October meeting. The September hike was justified partly on regional reports of pass-through; this is where that gets updated.
August's +39,500 against 20,000 expected is what tipped the RBA into a September hike. Unemployment was 4.6%; UBS thinks it needs to reach about 5% to bring inflation back.
4.6% last month, headline 5.4%. Pipeline pressure the Fed has been pointing at.
August rose 1.2% with the control group up 1.4%. Nominal sales are being flattered by fuel prices; the control group strips that out.
At the IMF meetings. Bailey has said high energy prices make a hold harder to maintain; Catherine Mann says a hike is needed and markets discount about 30bp of tightening by the end of the year.
4.3% in the second quarter. The one large economy still not fighting inflation reports the morning after a fortnight of holiday-thinned data.
3.0% in August against a 2% target with core at 2.4%. The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% for seven meetings and has an October hike about 59% priced; this lands ten days before it decides.
4.9% last time, the highest in years, against a Bank of England that has turned hawkish on energy. The labour market is the argument against a November hike; this is the last read before it.

3.1% last month with core 2.6%. The last inflation print before the Bank of England's November meeting, which is about 80% priced for a hike; Bailey has said high energy prices make the hold harder to maintain.

events.event: Euro area HCOB manufacturing PMI, flash (Oct)
events.note: The first October survey, the week before the ECB meets on the 29th. September's composite was the strongest in years with the energy bill in the input-price line; October's tells whether the bond sell-off has reached orders.

events.event: UK S&P Global composite PMI, flash (Oct)
US S&P Global manufacturing PMI, flash (Oct)
events.note: September's flash at 57.0 moved the ten-year 14.6bp on the day; this is the October read, five days before the FOMC.

Two days before the ECB meets. With French yields near 5% and the euro at a 17-month low, the survey's read on credit standards is the one hard data point on whether the bond sell-off has reached lending.
September's 81.9 was the lowest since 2014. The day before the FOMC decision begins.
The last print before the RBA's November meeting, after a 25bp hike on 29 September that took the cash rate to 4.60%. August was 4.0%; the trimmed mean below is the part the Board watches.
The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% for seven meetings; it publishes a policy report with this decision. Its minutes flag oil pass-through, and an October hike has been priced at about 59%.

events.event: BoC monetary policy report and statement

events.note: Released with the decision. The vote count and any change to the language on further firming are the read; September's vote was 12–0.

The first meeting since the 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00% on 16 September. After soft payrolls and PCE a second move is priced at about 19–20%, with December about 85%; the 24-year high in the ten-year and Tuesday's 4.932% three-year auction are the counterweights.
The first read of the third quarter, a day after the Fed decides. August's record imports have already cut estimates: Capital Economics says growth will come in below its 4.0% forecast, nearer 2.5%.

The deposit rate is 2.50% after the 10 September hike. Pricing has moved from three and a half further hikes to about two and a half on French bond stress and slower growth; one house expects a pause in October and a final 25bp hike in December. The accounts out today show how the last hike was argued.

Published the morning of the Bank of Japan's decision day. Core excluding food and energy was 3.0% last time; sources say the Bank may judge underlying inflation to have reached 2% in its outlook report.

howToRead.title: Impact is about how much price moves, not how much the number matters
howToRead.text: A high-impact release is one where the spread widens, liquidity thins and the first move often reverses. That is a statement about market structure at 08:30, not about economics. Plenty of important data is marked medium because the market has already priced it.

howToRead.title: The forecast is the level that matters, not the previous
howToRead.text: Price reacts to the gap between actual and forecast, not to whether a number went up or down. A 5.3% PPI print against a 5.3% forecast is a non-event; the same print against a 4.7% forecast is not.

howToRead.title: Two releases at the same minute are one event
howToRead.text: Agencies batch their releases, so you will often see three or four rows sharing a print time — jobless claims alongside the Philadelphia Fed, import prices alongside retail sales. Nobody trades the smaller one on a morning like that. When you see the same time twice, read the highest-impact row and ignore the others.

howToRead.title: A release-driven wick is not displacement
howToRead.text: Models built on liquidity runs misfire badly on data prints, because the move has no intent behind it — it is an auction gap. If your playbook has no rule about scheduled releases, this page is the argument for adding one.
